title: Shopping: du, de la, des
topic: partitive articles; de after negation and quantities
why: This is the key lesson on partitive articles: du, de la, de l', des for “some”, and plain de after a negation or a quantity. You'll use them in the little ritual of French shops, at the bakery and at the market.

{"lessons": ["

Some bread, some jam: du, de la, des

In English you can say “I'd like bread” or “I'd like some bread”. In French, a noun almost never stands alone: when you talk about an unspecified quantity of something (“some”, “any”, or nothing at all in English), you use a partitive article.

PartitiveExample
masculinedudu pain, du fromage
femininede lade la confiture, de la salade
before a vowel or a silent hde l'de l'eau, de l'huile
pluraldesdes tomates, des œufs
Je voudrais du pain, de la confiture et de l'eau.I'd like (some) bread, (some) jam and (some) water.

Compare with what you already know. Un croissant: one croissant, something you count. Du pain: some bread, a quantity you don't count. Le pain: bread in general, or a specific bread; the next lesson looks closely at this contrast.

You've met du and des as contractions (le prix du pain, the price of bread). The partitive looks the same but means “some”. And the du of faire du sport? It was a partitive all along. The typical English speaker's mistake is to drop it: “je voudrais pain” is impossible in French.

Des is also the plural of un / une: un œuf, des œufs. Either way, it translates as “some” or nothing at all: J'achète des tomates = I'm buying (some) tomatoes.

", "

Pas de, beaucoup de: when the article disappears

After a negation

After ne… pas, du, de la, de l', des and un, une all become de, or d' before a vowel. It's the English “not any” or “no”:

Je n'ai pas de lait. Il n'y a pas d'œufs.I don't have any milk. There are no eggs.
Tu veux de la salade ? — Non merci, je ne veux pas de salade.Do you want some lettuce? — No thanks, I don't want any lettuce.

One exception: after ce n'est pas, the article stays: Ce n'est pas du sucre, c'est du sel ! (That's not sugar, it's salt!)

After a quantity

After a word of quantity, French uses de alone, with no article, just like English “of” in “a kilo of tomatoes”.

FrenchEnglish
un kilo de tomatesa kilo of tomatoes
200 grammes de fromage200 grams of cheese
une bouteille de vina bottle of wine
un paquet de pâtesa packet of pasta
une douzaine d'œufsa dozen eggs
beaucoup de mondelots of people
un peu de sucrea little sugar
assez de painenough bread
trop de seltoo much salt

The classic trap is “beaucoup des”: it's always beaucoup de, even in the plural: beaucoup de tomates. And English “a dozen eggs” has no “of”, but French needs it: une douzaine d'œufs.

", "

At the market and the bakery

Shopping in France follows a little ritual, with set phrases on both sides of the counter. Shopkeepers say vous, and you always start with Bonjour !

WhoFrenchEnglish
ShopkeeperBonjour, vous désirez ?Hello, what would you like?
CustomerJe voudrais une baguette et deux croissants.I'd like a baguette and two croissants.
ShopkeeperEt avec ça ?Anything else?
CustomerVous avez des tartes aux fraises ?Do you have strawberry tarts?
ShopkeeperCe sera tout ?Will that be all?
CustomerC'est tout, merci. Ça fait combien ?That's all, thanks. How much is it?
ShopkeeperÇa fait six euros vingt.That comes to six euros twenty.

Ce sera tout ? uses a future form: take it as a fixed phrase for now.

Where to buy what

  • la boulangerie (the bakery): une baguette, un croissant, un pain au chocolat
  • la fromagerie (the cheese shop): du fromage, du beurre, des yaourts
  • le marché (the market): des tomates, des pommes, des fraises, de la salade, des pommes de terre (potatoes)

At the market, you can ask for a weight (un kilo de pommes, cinq cents grammes de fraises) or a number (trois tomates). And une salade is usually a head of lettuce, not a prepared salad.
